seoTitle: Free CSS Specificity Calculator: Which Selector Wins
metaDescription: Calculate CSS specificity as (a,b,c) for selectors or a whole stylesheet and see which one wins. Free, runs in your browser, nothing is uploaded.
intro: Computes the specificity of each CSS selector as an (a,b,c) triple and highlights the highest. Paste selectors one per line, as comma lists, or a full stylesheet.
why:
When your CSS rule has no effect, the cause is almost always specificity: a more specific selector somewhere else is winning. Working it out means counting IDs, classes and element names in your head, and remembering that :not() and :is() take their most specific argument while :where() counts for nothing.

Paste your selectors and each one is scored as three numbers: IDs, then classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, then elements and pseudo-elements. The highest is marked. You can paste a whole stylesheet, and the tool pulls out the selectors for you. Note that it compares selector specificity only, not source order, cascade layers or !important, which can also decide a conflict. It runs in your browser.
howTo: Paste selectors, one per line, or a whole stylesheet.
Read the (a,b,c) score in front of each selector.
Look for the line marked as the highest.

faq.a: The first number counts ID selectors, the second counts classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, the third counts element types and pseudo-elements. Compare from left to right: any higher a beats any b, and so on.
:not, :is, :matches and :has take the specificity of their most specific argument. :where adds nothing. nth-child pseudo-classes count as one class, plus any selector listed after "of".

faq.q: Does the tool consider !important, inline styles or layers?
faq.a: No. It scores selectors only. Inline styles, !important declarations, cascade layers and source order are applied separately by the browser and can override these results.

faq.q: What does the highest marker mean?
faq.a: It points at the selector with the greatest specificity in the list you pasted. If two are equal, the first one is shown, and in a real page the later rule in the source would win.
